title: Stories of the Prophets
author: Ibn Kathir (Ismail ibn Umar ibn Kathir)
standard_edition_analyzed: Islamic Foundation Publishing, English translation by Rashid Ahmad Azmi
target_audience: Muslims seeking to learn about the prophets in Islam
Students and scholars of Islamic theology and history
General readers interested in Abrahamic religious narratives
Parents and educators teaching Islamic history to children
core_themes: Monotheism and the message of God
Struggles and perseverance of the prophets
Continuity between prophets and their messages
primary_purpose: To recount and explain stories of the major prophets according to Islamic tradition, drawing from the Qur’an, hadith, and earlier sources, with the aim of teaching moral lessons, strengthening faith, and illuminating Islamic history through the lives and missions of God’s chosen messengers.

structure_format.organization: Divided by the stories of individual prophets, beginning with Adam and ending with Jesus (Isa, peace be upon him) and Muhammad (peace be upon him), each section outlining the life, character, and missions of the respective prophet.
features: Direct quotations from the Qur’an and hadith
Commentary and reflections by Ibn Kathir

key_concepts_lessons: Faithfulness and obedience to God are recurring values in prophetic stories.
Each prophet encountered unique challenges but remained steadfast in their mission.
Stories demonstrate God’s mercy, justice, and wisdom through trials and miracles.
Lessons are intended for spiritual reflection and emulation in everyday life.
Prophets are human beings chosen for revelation and guidance, not divine themselves.
Prophetic history provides context for key Islamic beliefs and practices.
notable_features: Compilation of prophetic stories from the Qur’an and early Islamic sources
Recognized as one of the most comprehensive classical works on the subject
Frequently referenced in sermons, classes, and Islamic literature
Bridges scriptural, historical, and moral insights
cultural_historical_context: Composed in the Mamluk period in Syria, Ibn Kathir’s 'Stories of the Prophets' addresses both scholarly and lay audiences, synthesizing material from the Qur’an, hadith, and earlier historians. It remains one of the most widely read and cited Islamic books outside the Qur’an and Hadith collections, often used to teach Islamic history and moral lessons to Muslims of all ages.
reception_impact: Canonical status in Islamic education and popular literature
Extensively translated and adapted for children and adults alike
Praised for its fidelity to Qur’anic text and clear exposition
Serves as an important reference for comparative Abrahamic studies
comparable_titles: Qasas al-Anbiya (The Stories of the Prophets) by al-Tha’labi
Lives of the Prophets by Imam Ibn Jarir al-Tabari
The Prophets by Syed Abul Hasan Ali Nadwi
